stories.headline: Todd Russell, Beaconsfield mine collapse survivor, dies aged 54 due to illness
stories.claim: Todd Russell, a survivor of the 2006 Beaconsfield mine collapse in Tasmania, has died aged 54 from illness.
stories.summary: Todd Russell, one of two miners trapped for about two weeks after the 2006 Beaconsfield gold mine collapse in Tasmania, has died aged 54. He had announced in early November that he was returning home to spend his remaining time with family and friends, after years of treatment for an undisclosed illness. Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese led tributes, recognising his resilience and his later work as a fire brigade chief and mental health advocate. The 2006 disaster killed miner Larry Knight and became a national event in Australia.
key_points: Todd Russell died aged 54, announced by Tasmanian officials on Tuesday 10 November.
He was one of two miners found alive after the 2006 Beaconsfield collapse and freed after 321 hours underground.
Russell had begun hospital treatment for an undisclosed illness in 2025 and returned home earlier this month.
He spoke openly about PTSD and depression and became a mental health advocate.
Premier Jeremy Rockliff and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese paid tribute; he served with the Beaconsfield fire brigade until February this year.

stories.headline: NASA keeps its PROMISE to raid Mars testbeds for parts
stories.claim: NASA is proceeding with PROMISE, a lunar rover repurposed from Mars engineering hardware, to land on the Moon by late 2028 for under $400 million.
stories.summary: NASA confirmed at a weekend briefing that it will repurpose engineering test hardware from the Mars rover programmes into a lunar rover called PROMISE, targeting a landing on the Moon's south pole by late 2028 for an 18-month mission. Blue Origin will deliver the rover using its Mark 1 lander under a $94 million base contract, with a further option worth up to $140 million. NASA says the total cost, including the lander, should stay under $400 million, which is far below an earlier outside estimate of at least $723 million. Critics note the figures are hard to verify and that the plan may strain engineering morale at JPL.

stories.headline: The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity
stories.claim: Analysis argues the US data-centre backlash is driven mainly by electricity supply and grid strain, not just culture-war politics.
stories.summary: Writing from Ashburn in Virginia's Data Center Alley, the MIT Technology Review argues the public backlash against data centres is largely about electricity rather than a culture war. Loudoun County data centres mostly connect to the grid, with Dominion Energy supplying power largely from natural gas. Newer rural AI campuses often bring their own gas turbines or diesel generators because local grids cannot supply them. New Virginia rules require data centres to pay the full cost of new transmission lines, and developers expect possible curbs during peak demand. The author argues the industry's power needs, not public opposition, are the main constraint on expansion.
key_points: The average Loudoun County data centre has about 54 megawatts of capacity, and most connect to Dominion Energy's grid.
Virginia has introduced rules requiring data centres to pay fully for new transmission lines.
Developers expect new rules that could cut them off from grid power during peak demand.
Large AI campuses often use on-site gas turbines, which release air pollutants.
Anthropic has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines, according to the article.
The author argues electricity supply is a bigger constraint on AI expansion than public opposition.
stories.market_take: Power and gas-turbine suppliers could benefit from the shift to on-site generation.

stories.headline: The Children's Place Commences Process to Effectuate Value-Maximizing Sale Transaction – Company Announcement
stories.claim: The Children's Place (PLCE) filed for US Chapter 11 bankruptcy and is running a sale of substantially all its assets.
stories.summary: The US children's clothing retailer The Children's Place, which owns the Gymboree brand, voluntarily filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in New Jersey on 8 November 2026. stories.claim: California voters rejected Proposition 40, a one-time 5% tax on billionaires' wealth, according to an AP race call.

Google co-founder Sergey Brin led heavy spending against it, at least five times the amount spent in favour.

stories.headline: What ‘catastrophic’ South Africa local election results mean for ANC
stories.claim: The ANC recorded its worst-ever local election result in South Africa, falling to 31% and losing the lead in key cities to the DA.
stories.summary: South Africa's ruling African National Congress recorded its worst result ever in local elections, winning about 31% of the vote against roughly 25% for the Democratic Alliance. The ANC lost its position as the largest party in Johannesburg, Pretoria and Ekurhuleni to the DA, while the DA kept Cape Town. The result is sharply down from 46% in 2021 and 66% in 2006. Because no party won a majority in many cities, the ANC and DA must negotiate coalitions within 14 days, and ANC secretary-general Fikile Mbalula called the result catastrophic. Analysts say the vote confirms a shift away from one-party dominance.

Federal proposals by Bernie Sanders and Ro Khanna remain under discussion.

stories.headline: Trump says war with Iran 'effectively over' after meeting Qatar PM
stories.claim: Trump says the war with Iran is militarily 'effectively over' and that talks show positive momentum toward ending it.
stories.summary: US President Donald Trump told reporters on Monday that Iran was militarily 'effectively over', after meeting Qatar's prime minister at the White House. He said Iran had been 'decapitated' but that a long-term solution to its nuclear programme was still needed. Trump said there was 'positive momentum' toward ending the war, without giving details, and that resumed strikes were 'highly unlikely' if a strong agreement is signed. He also said 38 bridges were identified as infrastructure targets if military action resumes. The US military has still carried out limited strikes on Iranian air defences in the past week and disabled a commercial ship trying to breach the US naval blockade of Iranian ports. The comments follow Republican losses in last week's midterm elections, where voter dissatisfaction with the eight-month-old war and surging fuel prices played a role.

stories.headline: Insight about how 'nature makes no leaps' promises better robot predictions
stories.claim: Researchers propose counterfactual world models that let robots predict what would have happened under other actions.
stories.summary: Researchers including Randall Balestriero, Kerda Varaku and Yann LeCun have published a pre-print paper proposing counterfactual world models, which let robots reason about actions they did not take. The method uses the gap between prediction and observed outcome to infer hidden factors, such as a current affecting a boat, and then predicts alternative actions. In simulated tasks, a robot using the approach reached its goal in 35 to 69 percent of events, against 14 to 23 percent for a planner ignoring the observed outcome. The approach uses off-the-shelf encoders with a small trained predictor. The work is a pre-print and has not been peer reviewed.
key_points: The pre-print paper is titled 'Counterfactual World Models: Natura Non Facit Saltus'.
The method uses the difference between predicted and actual outcomes to infer hidden disturbances.
In simulated tasks, success rose to 35 to 69 percent, against 14 to 23 percent for a baseline planner.
With two more attempts on the same event, success rose to 51 to 97 percent in the authors' tests.
The approach uses existing encoders such as DINOv2 and MAE with only a small predictor trained on top.
The authors claim the method is provably limited in error, but the work is at pre-print stage and not peer reviewed.

One iMessage bug could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages, and another exposed messages sent before a user joined. Prime Minister Rob Jetten, who joined an earlier march but not this one, said his government is increasing diplomatic pressure on Israel while also pressing Hamas.

stories.summary: On 3 November, voters in Upper Sandusky, Ohio, a town of about 6,600 people, approved by nearly 77% a measure banning large data centres within city limits. The ban followed months of opposition to a proposed roughly $900 million data centre and 150-megawatt natural gas power plant from Smartland Energy. Organisers first thought they needed 155 signatures for the ballot, then collected 301, but many were rejected and they were still short at the deadline. The case is an example of local communities pushing back against AI infrastructure. It is a local US story with limited market impact.
key_points: Voters in Upper Sandusky, Ohio, approved a ban on large data centres on 3 November.
Nearly 77% of voters backed the measure.
The ban targeted a proposed $900 million data centre and gas power plant by Smartland Energy.
The project would have covered about 146 acres and included a 150-megawatt gas plant.
Organisers struggled with rejected petition signatures before the ballot deadline.
stories.market_take: Local opposition to data centres could slow some AI infrastructure projects, but the impact here is small.

stories.headline: Physicists listened to electrical noise to crack a superconductor mystery
stories.claim: Physicists report evidence that electron pairing in cuprate superconductors begins at the pseudogap energy, before superconductivity sets in.
stories.summary: A team led by Milan Allan of LMU Munich and Ingmar Swart of Utrecht University, publishing in Science, has used shot noise measurements to study cuprate superconductors. Using a scanning tunnelling microscope on BSCCO crystals cooled to a few degrees above absolute zero, they found extra noise from paired electrons starting at the pseudogap energy. The effect vanished when magnetic fields up to six tesla suppressed pairing, supporting the pair explanation. The results suggest pairs form first and phase coherence sets in only at lower temperatures, so the bottleneck is getting pairs to move together. The researchers say this could in principle help raise the superconducting temperature.

stories.headline: The Binance hack offers a glimpse into the future of money
stories.claim: Commentary: the Binance hack's frozen funds show stablecoin issuers can enforce freezes across borders, raising questions about future money.
stories.summary: Telegraph columnist Izabella Kaminska argues that the roughly $6.3bn (about £4.7bn) Binance hack, widely attributed to North Korea, is notable less for its size than for how much stolen money was frozen. Stablecoin issuers Tether and Circle froze over $1.5bn and more than $1.1bn respectively, and Binance reported about $2.85bn frozen or intercepted by 3 November. She contrasts this with debates over Russia's frozen sovereign assets and the limits of traditional banking enforcement. She argues that the old model of negotiating a new monetary order, such as Bretton Woods, is too slow when hostile actors can exploit negotiations, and suggests rules should be built and tested iteratively like internet protocols.
key_points: The Binance hack, on 29 October, was about $6.3bn and is widely attributed to North Korea.
Tether said it froze more than $1.5bn within 30 minutes of discovery; Circle raised its freeze to over $1.1bn.
By 3 November, Binance reported roughly $2.85bn frozen or intercepted.
The author says stablecoin issuers can act across jurisdictions in ways banks struggle to, though some funds, such as Bitcoin, remain out of reach.
Freezing carries legal risks for issuers, and the column raises the wider question of how to rebuild the monetary system.
The piece is an opinion column rather than a reported news story.

stories.headline: The Fridge-Hacking Spree Is an Internet-of-Things Wake-Up Call
stories.claim: A wave of cyberattacks on connected fridges has disrupted blood storage and supermarkets across Europe and US bases.
stories.summary: Attacks on internet-connected refrigerators have affected three French sites that handle blood and plasma, where the Établissement Français du Sang confirmed on 2 November that cold rooms were raised to very high temperatures. Samples were not damaged because alarms and staff responded quickly. The attacks also hit supermarket chains in at least 11 European countries, earlier French stores in October, and US military commissaries in August. Many attacks appear to exploit vulnerable temperature controllers made by Danfoss. Responsibility is unclear: Russian hacktivists claimed some attacks without evidence, the Kremlin denied involvement, and US officials suspect Iran-linked actors in the US base incidents. The US CISA has issued an alert.

Attacks have also hit supermarket chains in at least 11 European countries, with food thrown away.
Similar incidents hit hundreds of French stores in October and US military commissaries in August.
Many attacks reportedly exploit vulnerable temperature controllers made by Danish firm Danfoss, which says systems ran outdated firmware.
The US CISA issued an alert; Sweden's National Cyber Security Center also issued advice.
Attribution is unclear: hacktivists claimed some attacks without evidence, the Kremlin denied involvement, and US officials suspect Iran-linked actors in the base incidents.
stories.market_take: Limited direct market effect; could raise demand for cybersecurity and cold-chain security, with Danfoss exposed to reputational questions.

stories.headline: State propaganda in some Chinese AI models is only "a thin layer" that fine-tuning can strip away
stories.claim: Nous Research released Arete-27B, a fine-tuned Qwen model it says removes Chinese state propaganda with little loss of capability.
stories.summary: US AI startup Nous Research fine-tuned Alibaba's Qwen3.8-27B on about 53 million tokens to reduce Chinese state propaganda in its answers. The resulting open-weight model, Arete-27B, cut the propaganda rate from 22% to 0.9% and raised its factual accuracy score from 2.32 to 2.98 out of 5 on the company's own 803-prompt test. Nous says general capabilities are largely preserved, though its benchmark results are self-reported and one gain is not claimed as real. The weights and dataset are released under an Apache 2.0 licence. The company recently raised $90 million at a $1.5 billion valuation.

He argues that AI now automates much of the attack chain, finding and exploiting bugs in real time, and points to the Chinese open-source tool ARTEX as an example. He expects a difficult adjustment period, or 'dark age', before defences catch up.

stories.headline: Court rules against Home Office in asylum seeker kidnapping case
stories.claim: Court of Appeal rejects Home Office view that kidnap for ransom is not trafficking exploitation.
stories.summary: The Court of Appeal has rejected the Home Office's argument that being kidnapped for ransom does not count as exploitation under trafficking rules. The case involved a 25-year-old Syrian asylum seeker who was abducted in Libya in 2021 and held for a month until his family paid a ransom. The Home Office had rejected his trafficking claim because he had not been forced into labour. The judges found the home secretary erred in not considering whether kidnapping amounted to exploitation. The ruling could allow many previously rejected people to seek fresh trafficking decisions, and the Home Office has said it is simplifying protection routes.

stories.headline: The Bantu expansion changed Africa. Scientists are still tracing how.
stories.claim: Scientists are using genetics, linguistics and archaeology to trace the Bantu expansion across Africa.
stories.summary: An Ars Technica feature explains how researchers from linguistics, archaeology and genetics are reconstructing the Bantu expansion, one of the largest human migrations in history. Bantu speakers, who likely began spreading from western Africa 4,000 to 6,000 years ago, brought farming, livestock, pottery and ironworking to southern and eastern Africa. Around 350 million people speak a Bantu language today. Genetic studies, including a 2024 analysis of 1,763 Africans, point to the Grassfields region of Cameroon as the probable homeland. stories.headline: Anthropic pushes ahead with pre-Thanksgiving IPO despite tech selloff, accepts lower valuation
stories.claim: Anthropic reportedly plans a pre-Thanksgiving IPO raising $80–100bn at a $1.25–1.75tn valuation, below earlier hopes.
stories.summary: According to investors cited by the Financial Times, Anthropic is pressing ahead with an IPO before Thanksgiving, accepting a lower valuation than its most optimistic backers hoped for. The company reportedly wants to raise $80 to $100 billion at a valuation of $1.25 to $1.75 trillion, compared with the $965 billion figure cited as its current value and the $2 trillion some investors had hoped for. Annualised revenue is reported at about $81 billion, up from roughly $65 billion at the end of July. The plan comes amid a tech selloff driven by rising borrowing costs, heavy AI spending and the Democratic midterm wins, which investors fear could slow data centre construction. The Nasdaq 100 fell 6.4 percent on Thursday before partly recovering on Friday. OpenAI has also reportedly cut its funding-round target to $1.25 trillion from $1.4 trillion and raised only about a third of the $30 billion it sought.

stories.headline: Are Europeans saving enough for retirement? Here is how much more they need to put aside
stories.claim: OECD Pensions Outlook 2026 finds most European mandatory pensions fall short of its 70% retirement income target.
stories.summary: The OECD's Pensions Outlook 2026 estimates how much extra employees on average wages would need to save voluntarily to retire on 70% of gross pay. Mandatory pensions fall short of the target in 22 of the 30 European countries studied. Lithuania has the largest gap as a share of earnings at 20.7%, while Switzerland has the highest monthly amount, above €1,000 for men on average wages. The UK gap is 9.1%, equal to about €494 a month, and France's is 6.2%, about €238 a month. Experts link the differences to the level of state pension provision, with lower replacement rates requiring more private saving. The projections include already-legislated retirement age rises.
